claim: Ash dieback is a disease caused by the fungal pathogen Hymenoscyphus fraxineus.
source: Ash dieback is a disease caused by the fungal pathogen Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, and it has devastated populations of ash trees (Fraxinus excelsior) across Europe in recent years.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as established fact about the disease.

claim: Hymenoscyphus fraxineus has devastated populations of ash trees (Fraxinus excelsior) across Europe in recent years.
source: Ash dieback is a disease caused by the fungal pathogen Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, and it has devastated populations of ash trees (Fraxinus excelsior) across Europe in recent years.
evidence: This is stated as a factual observation about the impact of the disease.

claim: Ash dieback was discovered in the wild in the east of England for the first time in 2012.
source: When ash dieback was discovered in the wild in the east of England for the first time, in 2012, the present authors set up the OpenAshDieBack (OADB) project as a crowdsourcing platform to allow scientists across the world to contribute to the genomic analysis of the pathogen and the host (MacLean et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a specific historical fact cited with a reference to MacLean et al., 2013.

claim: The OpenAshDieBack (OADB) project was set up as a crowdsourcing platform to allow scientists across the world to contribute to the genomic analysis of the pathogen and the host.
source: When ash dieback was discovered in the wild in the east of England for the first time, in 2012, the present authors set up the OpenAshDieBack (OADB) project as a crowdsourcing platform to allow scientists across the world to contribute to the genomic analysis of the pathogen and the host (MacLean et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the purpose of the OADB project with citation support.

claim: Fraxinus is a Facebook-based game developed to allow non-specialists to improve genetic variant predictions from DNA sequence data arising from the OADB project.
source: Subsequently, we developed and released Fraxinus, a Facebook-based game, to allow non-specialists to improve genetic variant predictions from DNA sequence data arising from the OADB project (MacLean, 2013).
evidence: This describes the purpose and platform of the Fraxinus game with citation.

claim: DNA sequence alignment is a hard problem that seeks to arrange two or more genome sequences in order to identify regions of similarity.
source: DNA sequence alignment is a hard problem that seeks to arrange two or more genome sequences in order to identify regions of similarity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DNA sequence alignment.

claim: When short fragments are being aligned with a longer sequence, the longer sequence is often considered to be a reference sequence that should not be altered.
source: When short fragments are being aligned with a longer sequence, the longer sequence is often considered to be a reference sequence that should not be altered.
evidence: This describes standard practice in sequence alignment.

claim: The process of alignment requires the best overall match between the two sequences to be found first through 'global alignment' followed by 'local alignment' that involves modifying the short sequences.
source: The process of alignment requires the best overall match between the two sequences to be found first: this 'global alignment' is then followed by a finer-grained 'local alignment' that involves modifying the short sequences by, for example, inserting small gaps or deleting short stretches of the sequence.
evidence: This describes the standard two-step alignment process.

claim: Alignment is a computationally intensive process.
source: Alignment is a computationally intensive process, and many computer programs (e.g., BWA aligner [Li and Durbin, 2009]) have been devised that implement and optimize alignments according to various measures of similarity.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of alignment with citation to BWA aligner.

claim: Many computer programs have been devised that implement and optimize alignments according to various measures of similarity.
source: Alignment is a computationally intensive process, and many computer programs (e.g., BWA aligner [Li and Durbin, 2009]) have been devised that implement and optimize alignments according to various measures of similarity.
evidence: This is stated with BWA aligner cited as an example.

claim: Percent identity is a straightforward measure of alignment similarity in which the number of identical nucleotides in the alignment is calculated as a proportion of whole alignment length.
source: A straightforward measure is percent identity (in which the number of identical nucleotides in the alignment is calculated as a proportion of whole alignment length).
evidence: This defines a standard metric used in sequence alignment.

claim: Once the alignment process is complete, any differences between the two sequences can be considered a genetic variation.
source: Once the alignment process is complete, any differences between the two sequences can be considered a genetic variation.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of alignment results.

claim: Genetic variations can be single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), in which a single nucleotide differs, or insertion–deletion polymorphisms (INDELs), in which longer stretches are different.
source: These differences can be single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), in which a single nucleotide differs, or insertion–deletion polymorphisms (INDELs), in which longer stretches are different.

claim: Software like SAMTools can identify the variants from alignments.
source: Software like SAMTools (Li et al., 2009) can identify the variants from alignments.
evidence: This states the capability of SAMTools with citation.
